## Background

Today we will explore some core machine learning methods that are very popular in bioinformatics. These include **clustering** and **dimensionallity reduction**.

## K-means

The main function in "base R" for K-means clustering is called `kmeans()`

Before we go too deep let's make up some "simple" data that we can cluster and know if we are getting good results or not. to do this we can use the `rnorm()` function:

```{r}
rnorm(10)
```

```{r}
hist( rnorm(100000) )
```

Give me 30 points centered at -3 and a second set with a mean of +3

```{r}
tmp <- c( rnorm(30, mean=-3), rnorm(30, mean=+3) )

x <- cbind(x=tmp, y=rev(tmp))
x
```

```{r}
plot(x)
```

Now try `kmeans()` on this input data `x`

```{r}
k <- kmeans(x, centers = 2)
k
```

To get to the results we can use `k$size` etc. to access each component result:

> Q. How many points are in each cluster?

```{r}
k$size
```

> Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster memebership?

```{r}
k$cluster
```

> Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster centers?

```{r}
k$centers
```

> Q. Make a results figure of our data with poitnts colored by cluster along with cluster centers.

```{r}
plot(x, col= c(1,2))
```

```{r}
plot(x,col=k$cluster)
points(k$centers, col="blue",pch=15)
```

> Q. Run kmeans again and cluster into 4 clusters producing a result figure with points colored by cluster and showing the cluster centers

```{r}
km <- kmeans(x, centers = 4)
plot(x,col=km$cluster)
points(km$centers, col="blue",pch=15)

```

> **N.B.** You need to tell k-means the number of clusters (i.e. set `centers=2`)!!

One approach is to try different values for `centers`and then pick the best one:

```{r}
ans <- NULL

for(i in 1:10) {
  #cat(i,"\n")
  km <- kmeans(x,centers = i)
  ans <- c(ans, km$tot.withinss)
}
```

```{r}
plot(ans, typ="o",
     xlab= "number of clusters",
     ylab= "Total sum of Squares Distance")
```

## Hierarchical Clustering

The main function in "base" R for Hierarchical Clustering is called `hclust()`

This function does not take your "raw" data for clustering. You must first build a "distance matrix" from your data and pass this as input for `hclust()`.

```{r}
d <- dist(x)
hc <- hclust(d)
hc
```

```{r}
plot(hc)
abline (h=8, col="red")
```

Once we have our `hclust` object (our "tree" or "cluster dendrogram") we can "cut" the tree to reveral the clustering pattern:

```{r}
cutree(hc, h=8)
```

You can use either `h=` or `k=` arguments to `cutree()`

```{r}
cutree(hc, k=4)
```

> Q. Make a plot of input data `x` with your clusters from `hclust()` (i.e. colored by cluster membership from cutting the tree)?

```{r}
grps <- cutree(hc,h=8)
plot(x, col = grps)
```

## Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is a dimensionality reduction method that is popular for revealing patterns in complex datasets.

### Analysis of UK food data

let's look at some data on eating habits of folks from the UK to see if there are patterns and trends that have some regions being distinct from others.

### Data import

The data is made available in CSV format so we can use `read.csv()`:

```{r}
x <- read.csv("https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods", row.names = 1)
x
```

> Q1. How many rows and columns are in your new data frame named x? What R functions could you use to answer this questions?

```{r}
nrow(x)
ncol(x)
```

> Q2. Which approach to solving the ‘row-names problem’ mentioned above do you prefer and why? Is one approach more robust than another under certain circumstances?

Setting row.names=1 inside read.csv() is the better choice. The other approach sets rownames(x) \<- x\[,1\] and then runs x \<- x\[,-1\], and that is destructive.

Some plots:

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=T, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```

> Q3.Changing what optional argument in the above barplot() function results in the following plot?

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=F, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))

```
Changing beside = TRUE to beside = FALSE (or F) turns the grouped barplot into the stacked one you have here.

> Q4. Changing what optional argument in the above ggplot() code results in a stacked barplot figure?

```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

x_long <- x |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Food") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -Food, names_to = "Country", values_to = "Consumption")

ggplot(x_long) +
  aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  theme_bw()
```
Change position = "dodge" to position = "stack"

### Pairs plots and heatmaps

One plot that can be useful for relatively small datasets is a `pairs()` plot:

> Q5. We can use the pairs() function to generate all pairwise plots for our countries. Can you make sense of the following code and resulting figure? What does it mean if a given point lies on the diagonal for a given plot?

```{r}
pairs(x, col=rainbow(nrow(x)), pch=16)
```
The two countries eat about the same amount of that food. A point above the diagonal means the y-axis country eats more of it, and a point below means the x-axis country eats more. England, Wales and Scotland plotted against each other sit fairly close to the diagonal, so their diets are broadly similar, with only a little scatter.

> **Key-point**: Even relatively small datasets can prove challenging to interpret

Given that it is quite difficult to make sense of even this relatively small data set. Hopefully, we can clearly see that a powerful analytical method is absolutely necessary if we wish to observe trends and patterns in larger datasets.

## PCA to the rescue!

The main function in "base" R for PCA is called `prcomp()`:

This function will require the transpose of our dataset

```{r}
pca <- prcomp( t(x) )
```

We can see how well or PCA results are doing in terms of the "Variance captured" from the original data in each PC.

```{r}
summary(pca)
```

I can see what is in my `pca` results object by:

```{r}
attributes(pca)
```

Of these `pca$x` is our main result. We can use it to make a results figure often called a PCA plot (or score- plot).

```{r}
pca$x
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(PC1,PC2) +
  geom_point(col=c("orange","red","blue","darkgreen"))

```

A "loadings" plot can show us how the original dimensions/variables contribute to our new PC axis. This is detailed in the `pca$rotation` component of our new result object:

```{r}
pca$rotation
```

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1,row.names(pca$rotation)) +
  geom_col()
```

> Q6. Based on the pairs and heatmap figures, which countries cluster together and what does this suggest about their food consumption patterns? Can you easily tell what the main differences between N. Ireland and the other countries of the UK in terms of this data-set?

England, Wales and Scotland cluster together, and N. Ireland is the outlier in both the pairs plot and the heatmap dendrogram. This suggests the three have similar diets while N. Ireland’s differs.

It is hard to say exactly how they differ from these plots alone. You can spot hints, such as more fresh potatoes and less fresh fruit and alcohol in NI, but it isn’t easy to pick out the main drivers. That difficulty is the reason the lab moves on to PCA.

> Q7. Complete the code below to generate a plot of PC1 vs PC2. The second line adds text labels over the data points.

```{r}
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = Country) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  xlim(-270, 500) + xlab("PC1") + ylab("PC2") + theme_bw()
```

> Q8. Customize your plot so that the colors of the country names match the colors in our UK and Ireland map and table at start of this document.

```{r}
mycols <- c("orange", "red", "blue", "darkgreen")  # England, Wales, Scotland, N.Ireland

ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = Country) +
  geom_point(size = 3, col = "grey") +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5, col = mycols) +
  xlim(-270, 500) + xlab("PC1") + ylab("PC2") + theme_bw()
```

> Q9: Generate a similar ‘loadings plot’ for PC2. What two food groups feature prominantely and what does PC2 maninly tell us about?

```{r}
load2 <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation)
load2$Food <- rownames(load2)

ggplot(load2) +
  aes(PC2, reorder(Food, PC2)) +
  geom_col() + xlab("PC2 Loading Score") + ylab("") + theme_bw()
```
Soft drinks has by far the largest positive PC2 loading. The bar cut off at the bottom is Fresh potatoes, with the largest negative loading. Scroll down or enlarge the plot window to see its label.
